hook: The traveller from Tangier who went farther than anyone before the age of steam.

pages.x: Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier, in Morocco, in 1304, into a family of judges. At 21 he set out alone on the pilgrimage to Mecca, leaving his parents in tears. He would not come home for 24 years.

After Mecca he kept going, with a rule never to travel the same road twice if he could help it. He crossed Iraq and Persia, sailed down the coast of East Africa to Kilwa, and rode across the steppes of the Golden Horde.

In India the sultan of Delhi, a brilliant but cruel ruler, made him a judge with a huge salary. He stayed seven years, until the sultan sent him as ambassador to China. His fleet was wrecked, and he lost everything.

In the Maldives he became chief judge and married into the royal family; he married about ten times on his travels. When he tried to make the easy-going islanders follow strict religious law, it did not go down well, and he soon left.

He reached China around 1345, landing at the great port of Quanzhou, then sailed for home. In Damascus he heard his father had died; in Morocco, that the Black Death had killed his mother. Later he crossed the Sahara to Mali and Timbuktu.

The sultan of Morocco had him tell his travels to a writer, Ibn Juzayy. The book, the Rihla, "The Journey", is one of the great travel books of all time, a priceless picture of the Muslim world of the 1300s.
Ibn Battuta travelled about 117,000 km over 30 years, through more than 40 of today's countries: farther than Marco Polo or anyone else before the age of steam.
pts: Saw nearly the whole Muslim world, India and China
Wrote one of the greatest travel books
